## Summary

Muscle near-infrared spectroscopy (mNIRS) is increasingly used in exercise physiology, sport science, and clinical rehabilitation for non-invasive assessment of local tissue oxygenation and metabolism during exercise. Wearable mNIRS devices have made data collection increasingly accessible outside specialised laboratory environments. However, processing and analysing mNIRS data remains fragmented. NIRS research groups and individual users commonly rely on custom scripts or manual spreadsheets developed ad-hoc over time, making analyses difficult to reproduce and standardise.

`mnirs` is an open-source R package for reading, processing, visualising, and analysing mNIRS time-series data. The package provides a standardised workflow covering common processing steps used for many mNIRS applications. `mnirs` can read files from multiple commercially available devices, clean invalid observations, resample, smooth data with digital filtering, shift and rescale multi-channel signals, extract intervals, and visualise data at every step of the processing pipeline. 

Along with a flexible R package, a companion web application provides access to a basic no-code workflow for NIRS users with minimal coding experience. `mnirs` is designed for researchers, practitioners, and individual NIRS users, emphasising accessibility, reproducibility, and transparent processing decisions.

## Statement of need

Near-infrared spectroscopy has been used in human physiology research for nearly fifty years to evaluate local oxygen delivery and extraction within biological tissue [@Jobsis1977]. In the past decade, wearable continuous-wave mNIRS devices have substantially expanded the use of this technology beyond specialised research laboratories into applied sport science, clinical practice, and field-based exercise physiology [@Grassi2016][@Perrey2024][@Jan2026].

While collecting mNIRS data is easier than ever, processing and analysing those data remains a challenge. NIRS signals are inherently noisy and sensitive to differences in tissue composition [@vanBeekvelt2001][@Stuer2024], unknown optical properties [@Hammer2019][@Priovano2021], and device-specific signal processing[@McManus2018][@Feldmann2026]. Continuous-wave CW-NIRS devices report relative changes in optical signals from an arbitrary baseline, and the resulting oxygenation signals are strongly influenced by processing decisions including filtering, interpolation, baseline correction, and normalisation (technical details and applications of NIRS can be found in @Barstow2019, @Hamaoka2019, and @Grassi2016). 

Consequently, laboratories and users frequently develop their own processing workflows tailored to the devices they have, and their particular research questions. In practice, these workflows often consist of in-house proprietary software, ad-hoc scripts, and manually edited spreadsheets. Processing decisions are frequently undocumented, or default parameters can be applied across NIRS devices with very different recording properties.

Such approaches are reasonable for individual projects, but they can stand in the way of multi-centre collaboration and make analyses difficult to share and reproduce. As mNIRS applications continue to expand, there is increasing value in providing transparent and standardised software to implement commonly performed processing methods.

The `mnirs` package was developed to reduce these barriers. The aim is to provide a collection of flexible R functions which allow researchers to implement processing pipelines appropriate for their own applications. Processed data then compatible with further analysis workflows with existing statistical and visualisation packages in the R ecosystem.

## State of the field

Some commercial mNIRS devices are distributed with proprietary software for real-time visualisation and basic signal processing (e.g. Oxysoft, Artinis, Elst, the Netherlands). Others allow for recording to a variety of apps and devices, or will simply export raw data from onboard recording (e.g. Moxy monitor, Fortiori Design LLC., Hutchinson, MN, USA). These commercially available mNIRS devices each export files in different formats, using various names for the common NIRS channels; e.g. SmO<sub>2</sub>, TSI, or StO<sub>2</sub> for an oxygen saturation value [@Feldmann2026].

Within R, software specifically developed for mNIRS processing remains limited. To our knowledge there is currently only one other R package listed on CRAN explicitly related to NIRS analysis [@Wang2020], which does not to be under active maintenance. `mnirs` is currently the only open-source, under active development CRAN package specifically developed to support the complete processing workflow for wearable mNIRS data.

Other biological and health science disciplines have broad representation on CRAN (e.g. biostatistics, ecology & environmental sciences, epidemiology, genetics, and many others) with packages that complement each other to advance and standardise methodology across the field. mNIRS research would benefit from additional open-source development of tools to help users work with data in R, Python, and other platforms.

## Software design

`mnirs` was released as version 0.6.0 on the comprehensive R archive network (CRAN). The official CRAN release can be downloaded directly in the R working environment by calling:

`install.packages("mnirs")`

The latest development version can be downloaded from:

`pak::pak("jemarnold/mnirs")`

The package website has comprehensive documentation of the functions discussed below, and includes vignettes demonstrating common mNIRS data processing pipelines:

`https://jemarnold.github.io/mnirs/articles/reading-mnirs-data.html`

An online app is available as a ‘no-code’ workflow with basic `mnirs` processing functionality, for rapid visualisation and comparison of processing methods:

`https://jemarnold-mnirs-app.share.connect.posit.cloud/`

`mnirs` is designed around an incremental processing pipeline:

```
read_mnirs()                             # read & import data from file
  ├─ plot()                              # visualise at each processing step 
  └─ resample_mnirs()                    # regularise or resample time grid
      └─ replace_mnirs()                 # clean invalid, outliers, missing
          └─ filter_mnirs()              # smooth with digital filtering
              ├─ shift_mnirs()           # shift multi-channel signals
              └─ rescale_mnirs()         # normalise multi-channel signal range
                  └─ extract_intervals() # extract for further analysis
```

`read_mnirs()` will typically be the first function called from `mnirs` to read a file exported from an mNIRS device, and return a data frame of class `"mnirs"` ready for further processing. This function will recognise files from most commercially available mNIRS devices, and can automatically detect the appropriate NIRS and time channels. These can be customised and renamed, and metadata (e.g. sample rate and recording start time) will be extracted if present and stored as attributes of the returned data frame. This allows subsequent `mnirs` functions to automatically detect and apply these values, rather than having to repeatedly specify them manually.

`plot.mnirs()` or the generic `plot()` can be called on `mnirs` data frames to visualise data at each processing step. Visual inspection is an important part of mNIRS processing decisions.

`resample_mnirs()` is used to up- or down-sample mNIRS data for synchronisation with other devices, or to regularise the time grid if a NIRS device records at an irregular sampling rate.

`replace_mnirs()` can detect and replace local outliers, invalid specific values, values outside of a valid range, and fill or interpolate across missing data.

`filter_mnirs()` can be used to apply several methods for smoothing, including simple moving average, a non-parametric smoothing spline, or fully parameterised digital filters. Filtering is one of the most important steps in processing mNIRS data to improve signal-to-noise ratio and capture relevant physiological signals. However, over-parameterised filtering can over-smooth the data and influence interpretations just as much as trying to analyse overly-noisy raw data. It is perfectly valid to choose a filter method by iteratively testing filter parameters until the signal or response of interest








The package is organised around the sequence of processing steps typically performed when working with mNIRS recordings. Rather than requiring users to adapt their workflow to a particular data structure, `mnirs` aims to simplify common tasks while remaining compatible with existing R workflows.

The first step is importing data from files exported by commercial mNIRS devices. Manufacturers use different file formats, channel names, and metadata structures, making data import unnecessarily time consuming when working across multiple devices. The read_mnirs() function automatically detects common file formats and channel names, extracts available metadata such as sampling frequency and recording time, and returns a standardised data frame. Metadata are stored alongside the imported data and are recognised automatically by subsequent processing functions, reducing the need to repeatedly specify channel mappings throughout an analysis.

Visual inspection is an important part of mNIRS processing. Processing decisions are often made iteratively by evaluating the effects of filtering, interpolation, or signal normalisation on the physiological response of interest. A generic plotting method is therefore provided so that imported and processed recordings can be visualised directly using plot(), while remaining fully compatible with further customisation using ggplot2.

Several functions implement common preprocessing operations applied to physiological time-series data. Invalid observations and obvious movement artefacts can be identified and replaced, with optional interpolation of missing values. Recordings can be resampled to regular sampling intervals or converted to different sampling frequencies to facilitate synchronisation with other physiological measurements, including metabolic gas exchange, heart rate, or electromyography. Signal smoothing is available using smoothing splines, Butterworth digital filters, or moving averages, allowing users to select processing methods appropriate for their sampling frequency and experimental application.

Signal shifting and rescaling are also provided because absolute values recorded by continuous-wave mNIRS devices are often not directly comparable between recording sessions, devices, muscle sites, or individuals. Different studies employ different normalisation strategies depending on the experimental question, including baseline correction, functional normalisation, or calibration using vascular occlusion protocols. Rather than enforcing a particular approach, `mnirs` provides flexible methods for shifting and rescaling either individual channels or groups of channels while preserving transparency regarding the processing decisions applied.

After preprocessing, analyses are commonly performed on specific periods of interest rather than entire recordings. Exercise bouts, recovery periods, or repeated vascular occlusions can therefore be extracted using event markers, lap counters, timestamps, or sample indices. Multiple extracted intervals may also be ensemble averaged to improve signal-to-noise ratio for repeated protocols, providing a common starting point for subsequent physiological modelling.

The package intentionally focuses on preprocessing rather than statistical analysis. Imported and processed recordings remain standard R data frames and therefore integrate directly with existing packages for modelling, visualisation, and reporting. This allows users to combine domain-specific mNIRS processing with the broader collection of statistical tools already available within R.

Accessibility

Although reproducible analyses are best achieved through scripted workflows, many researchers and practitioners using wearable mNIRS devices have limited programming experience. To improve accessibility, the core processing workflow implemented by `mnirs` is also available through a freely accessible web application.

The application allows users to upload exported recordings, compare different preprocessing methods, and visualise the effects of filtering and signal transformation without writing code. Because the application uses the same underlying package functions, workflows developed interactively can later be reproduced directly within R if required.

Documentation for the package is provided through a package website, function reference pages, and worked examples demonstrating common processing pipelines.


Future Development

Version 0.6 provides the core functionality required for reading and preprocessing mNIRS recordings. Future releases will extend the package to include higher-level analytical methods that are becoming increasingly common within exercise physiology and sport science, including oxygenation kinetics modelling, critical oxygenation breakpoint detection, and oxidative capacity analysis.

As an open-source project, future development will also be guided by contributions from the broader mNIRS community, including support for additional devices, improvements to existing workflows, and implementation of emerging analytical methods.

Conclusions

`mnirs` provides a reproducible workflow for reading, processing, and preparing muscle near-infrared spectroscopy data for analysis in R. By implementing commonly used preprocessing methods within an open-source framework, the package reduces reliance on laboratory-specific scripts and manual spreadsheet workflows while remaining flexible enough to support a wide range of experimental applications. The package is intended to complement existing statistical tools within R and to provide a common foundation upon which future community-developed methods for mNIRS analysis can be built.
